data.title: DB updater atomicity hardening: restore single-transaction chunk invariant
data.body:
## Goal

The pool updater's chunk loop has a **correctness regression** vs `main`: the "process complete chunk before commit" atomicity invariant was shattered during the migration of writes into the Rust core. Restore (and enforce structurally) a single-transaction-per-chunk so that an interrupt mid-chunk rolls the whole chunk back atomically — leaving `last_update_block` and the committed pool/liquidity data consistent.

## Background — the regression

On `main`, the chunk loop (`src/degenbot/cli/pool.py`) open was a **single atomic transaction**:
- One shared SQLAlchemy `session` threaded through every update call.
- Updaters did `session.add(...)` / `session.execute(...)` — never `commit()`.
- The `last_update_block` stamp was a dirty ORM attribute on the same session — uncommitted until chunk end.
- **One `session.commit()` at chunk end** durably persisted pool rows + liquidity updates + the stamp together. Ctrl-C mid-chunk → the whole transaction rolled back → `last_update_block` still pointed at the previous chunk end → restart re-processed the chunk cleanly with no duplicates.

In the current tree, the inner calls were migrated to the Rust core without preserving this invariant:
- `db_upsert_v3_pools` / `db_upsert_v2_pools` / `db_upsert_v4_pools` open their **own** connection via `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes`, and `upsert_v3_pools` (`rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs`) does **per-row autocommit `execute()` with no `transaction()` wrapper** — pool rows are durable immediately, mid-chunk, on a separate connection from the stamp.
- `db_apply_v3_liquidity_updates` / `db_apply_v4_liquidity_updates` — separate connection again.
- `db_set_exchange_last_update_block` — separate connection again.
- The `session.commit()` on the Python side now only commits whatever the SQLAlchemy session still owns (the stamp, partially), while the pool writes were already committed by Rust earlier.

**Consequence:** pool writes and the `last_update_block` stamp live in separate transactions on separate connections. An interrupt in the gap between "Rust commits the pools" and "Rust commits the stamp" → pools durably present, stamp stale → restart refetches the same `PoolCreated` events → `UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.address, pools.chain`. Worse: the `last_update_block` ground truth no longer actually bounds the committed pool data — this is a **correctness regression**, not just a duplicate-insert annoyance.

User-observed symptom: `uv run degenbot pool update` interrupted around block 12M, restarted → `ValueError: sqlite error: UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.address, pools.chain`.

## Scope

Restoring the invariant in a way that is **structurally enforced** (not just convention) and consistent with ADR-005 (Rust owns the writes; Python is a thin shell). The chunk's writes — pool upserts, liquidity updates, `last_update_block` stamp — must be a single SQLite transaction. An interrupt rolls back the whole chunk. Restart is idempotent.

This epic includes: (1) the research/invariant write-up that pins down the exact contract + names the approach; (2) the implementation tasks derived from that research.

## Out of scope

- Auto-heal-on-open (ADR-011 non-goals).
- The broader "move all DB interaction into Rust" program — only the pool updater chunk path is in scope here.
- Performance work unrelated to correctness.

data.title: Research: define the chunk-atomicity invariant + scope the Rust-owned chunk updater
data.body:
## Goal

Produce a precise write-up that (1) states the exact invariant the pool updater must hold, (2) names the concrete approach to restore it in the current Rust-core architecture, and (3) decomposes that approach into implementation tasks to attach to this epic. **The write-up IS this task's deliverable** — no code changes.

## Direction (already endorsed by the orchestrator)

**The whole chunk loop may move into Rust.** If the entire chunk (fetch events, upsert pools, apply liquidity updates, stamp `last_update_block`) is one Rust call, then Rust owns one connection + one transaction and the write/stamp desync is **structurally impossible** — there's only one writer. The PyO3 seam becomes something like `run_pool_update_chunk(database_path, chain_id, exchange specs, start_block, end_block, ...) -> ChunkReport`. This is the strongly-preferred direction (ADR-005: Rust is the engine; Python is a thin shell).

The research must confirm whether this is the right approach vs the partial fix (thread a single connection through the existing `db_*` seams without rewriting the loop) and name the trade-offs.

## What the write-up must establish

### 1. The invariant (state it precisely)

Pin down the exact contract, by reference to `main`:
- A "chunk" is a batch of blocks `[working_start_block, working_end_block]` processed atomically.
- **Atomicity invariant:** at chunk commit, EITHER (a) every pool row from `PoolCreated` events in the chunk + every liquidity update from `Mint`/`Burn` events in the chunk + the `last_update_block = working_end_block` stamp are ALL durably persisted (single transaction commit), OR (b) NONE of them are (single transaction rollback). No intermediate state is observable — including across an interrupt or crash.
- **Restart invariant:** `last_update_block` is a strict upper bound on the block range whose pool + liquidity data is durably committed. Restarting from `last_update_block + 1` re-processes only work that was NOT committed — never re-applies committed work.
- **No-duplicate-writer invariant:** at most one connection holds a write transaction on the DB during a chunk. (The current code violates this with multiple short-lived `DegenbotDb` connections + a SQLAlchemy session all writing concurrently.)

Reference the exact lines on `main` (git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py) where the invariant was held by construction: the shared `session` threaded through every updater, the ORM-dirty `exchange.last_update_block` stamp, the single `session.commit()` at chunk end.

### 2. The current regression (cite the code)

Document precisely how the invariant is broken in the current tree:
- `db_upsert_v3_pools` (and v2/v4) → own connection via `open_for_writes`; `upsert_v3_pools` (`rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs`) does per-row autocommit `execute()` with NO `transaction()` wrapper — pool rows durable mid-chunk, separate connection from the stamp.
- `db_apply_v3_liquidity_updates` / `db_apply_v4_liquidity_updates` — confirm the same pattern (separate connection; own writes). Read `rust/crates/degenbot-python/src/db/*.rs` for these seams.
- `db_set_exchange_last_update_block` — separate connection again.
- The SQLAlchemy `session.commit()` only commits SQLAlchemy-owned state, not the Rust writes.
- Net: writes + stamp live in separate transactions on separate connections → interrupttroduces write/stamp desync → the observed `UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.address, pools.chain`.

### 3. The approaches (name + evaluate)

Evaluate these in the write-up; pick one as THE approach (with rationale); the others are documented as considered-and-rejected:

**A. Move the whole chunk loop into Rust (preferred direction — confirm).** A Rust function (e.g. `pool_update_chunk(database_path, chain_id, exchange_specs, start_block, end_block, ...) -> ChunkReport`) owns the single connection + single transaction for the chunk: fetches events (or accepts pre-fetched events), upserts pools, applies liquidity updates, stamps `last_update_block`, commits once or rolls back. The PyO3 seam is one call; Python no longer holds a write-bearing session. This is the maximal Rust ownership answer and the structurally-safest.

  - Sub-questions to resolve in the write-up:
    - Does the chunk loop fetch RPC events in Rust or Python? (The current loop fetches via `get_events_from_contract` / `get_v3_liquidity_events` / `get_v4_liquidity_events` in Python, then passes results to the Rust write seams.) Recommend: keep RPC fetching in Python (it's I/O orchestration, the legitimate Python-shell responsibility), pass the decoded events INTO the Rust chunk function, and let Rust do all the DB writes + the commit in one transaction. The chunk function's signature should accept the decoded event payloads, not do RPC itself.
    - OR: push RPC into Rust too (bigger — needs the RPC crate work; only do if it's clearly the right call for atomicity, which it probably isn't — RPC is I/O, not DB state). Document.
    - How are the per-exchange `new_pool_events` + the cross-exchange `liquidity_events` batches combined into one transaction? (They're currently separate calls; the chunk function must accept them all + commit once.)

**B. Thread a single DegenbotDb connection through the existing `db_*` seams.** Expose a connection-scoped handle (e.g. a `DegenbotDb` clone or a `&Connection`-bearing wrapper) at the PyO3 level so the chunk loop can open one connection, pass it to `upsert_v3_pools` / `apply_v3_liquidity_updates` / `set_exchange_last_update_block`, and commit at chunk end. Smaller change than A.

  - Trade-off: the PyO3 seam gets more complex (connection handle is a new `#[pyclass]`); still leaves the chunk loop's orchestration in Python (which is fine for ADR-005's "thin shell" reading); must ensure a single transaction spans all calls (either explicit `BEGIN`..`COMMIT` or rusqlite `transaction()`).
  - Sub-question: is this even achievable cleanly given the current `DegenbotDb` is `Mutex<Connection>` and the `db_*` seams open-and-close per call? May need a "borrow connection" seam.

**C. Make the individual writes idempotent (`INSERT OR IGNORE` / `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) without fixing the transaction structure.** Rejected as a real fix: it papers over the duplicate-pool-insert symptom but leaves the write/stamp desync — `last_update_block` would still lag the committed pool data, and `apply_*_liquidity_updates` would double-apply Mint/Burn events (stateful — not idempotent — unlike pool inserts). Record as "considered and rejected: doesn't restore the invariant."

**D. Keep the chunk in Python, wrap everything in one DB-level `BEGIN`..`COMMIT`.** E.g. a PyO3 seam `db_begin_transaction(database_path) -> TxHandle` + `db_commit_transaction(tx)`. Rejected: leaking SQLite transaction handles across the PyO3 boundary is fragile (what if Python raises mid-chunk? the tx leaks; rollback semantics get murky). Record as considered-and-rejected.

### 4. The implementation task decomposition

After picking the approach (likely A), decompose into implementation tasks to file as children of this epic. Each task should be ~1 commit, with clear gates. For approach A, likely tasks (use as a starting sketch; refine in the write-up):

1. `pool_update_chunk` Rust core function — owns the single connection + transaction, accepts decoded events (new_pool_events per exchange + liquidity_events), does the pool upserts + liquidity updates + stamp + commit/rollback. Reuses existing `upsert_v*_pools` / `apply_*_liquidity_updates` / `set_exchange_last_update_block` logic but bound to the passed-in connection.
2. PyO3 seam — thin wrapper; GIL released across the chunk. Define the event-payload types (or accept the raw decoded values Python already produces).
3. Python chunk loop refactor — keep RPC fetching (the `get_events_*` calls) in Python; replace the per-exchange `pool_updater(...)` + per-pool `apply_*_liquidity_updates(...)` + the stamp loop with a single `run_pool_update_chunk(...)` call per chunk. Drop the SQLAlchemy `session.commit()` (the Rust function owns the commit now).
4. Remove the now-redundant standalone `db_upsert_v*_pools` / `db_apply_*_liquidity_updates` / `db_set_exchange_last_update_block` seams IF the chunk function supersedes them (or keep them for standalone testing + have the chunk function call into the same core logic without going through the seam). Decide + document.
5. A regression test that reproduces the bug: interrupt mid-chunk (mock the interrupt) → assert the chunk is fully rolled back → restart re-processes cleanly with no `UNIQUE constraint` failure. This is the contract artifact for the invariant.
6. (Maybe) a test that proves the no-duplicate-writer invariant: the chunk function holds a write transaction; a concurrent `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes` during the chunk blocks/refuses rather than producing concurrent writers.

These tasks should be filed as children of this epic with the dependencies sequenced. The orchestrator will create them from the write-up's decomposition.

## Deliverable

A markdown file at `docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md` capturing:
- The invariant (§1).
- The current regression (§2, with code citations).
- The approaches + the chosen approach + rationale (§3).
- The implementation task decomposition (§4) — concrete enough that the orchestrator can file the tasks directly from it.

Commit it as `docs(migration): define pool-updater chunk atomicity invariant + fix approach`. Reference epic `2SFL6I`. Reference `main`'s chunk loop as the contract source of truth.

## Constraints

- **Read `main` first** (`git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py`) — that's the contract. The current tree is the regression; `main` is the reference.
- Read the current Rust seams (`rust/crates/degenbot-python/src/db/*.rs`) + core (`rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs`, `connection.rs`) to cite the exact breakage points.
- No code changes in this task — the write-up is the deliverable. The implementation tasks (filed separately after this lands) do the code.
- Read ADR-005 (`docs/adr/ADR-005-polars-inspired-three-layer-architecture.md`) + the migration guide (`docs/migration-guides/three-layer-transition.md`) to ground "Rust is the engine" in the project's own architecture language.

## Report-back (to orchestrator t-6ff7 via link_send triggerTurn:true)

1. Commit hash of the write-up.
2. The chosen approach (A/B/C/D) + one-paragraph rationale.
3. The list of implementation tasks you decomposed (titles + one-line summaries) — so the orchestrator can file them as epic children.
4. Any sub-question from §3 you couldn't resolve + why.

## Goal

Produce a precise write-up that (1) states the exact invariant the pool updater must hold, (2) names the concrete approach to restore it in the current Rust-core architecture, and (3) decomposes that approach into implementation tasks to attach to this epic. **The write-up IS this task's deliverable** — no code changes.

## Direction (endorsed by the orchestrator)

**The whole chunk loop moves into Rust, and Python only starts the process.** Python's role is "boot the config, hand off the DB path + chain/exchange specs, start the update run" — NOT to drive each RPC read or DB write through FFI per call. The current per-call FFI dance (Python fetches events → calls `db_upsert_v3_pools` → `db_apply_v3_liquidity_updates` → `db_set_exchange_last_update_block`, each its own connection/transaction) is precisely the pattern to eliminate: it's both a bottleneck (repeated FFI + connection churn) and the root of the write/stamp desync regression.

The chunk loop — including RPC event fetching, pool upserts, liquidity updates, the `last_update_block` stamp, and the single chunk transaction — lives in Rust as one cohesive unit. The PyO3 seam is something like `run_pool_update(database_path, chain_id, exchange_specs, to_block, chunk_size, ...) -> UpdateReport`. Python boots the process and reports progress; Rust does everything else under one connection + one transaction per chunk.

This means the RPC fetching work (currently `get_events_from_contract` / `get_v3_liquidity_events` / `get_v4_liquidity_events` in Python, using `web3.py`) must ALSO move into Rust, OR be done by a Rust RPC layer that the chunk function calls. The research must confirm this + scope it.

- `db_set_exchange_last_update_block` — separate connection again.
- The SQLAlchemy `session.commit()` only commits SQLAlchemy-owned state, not the Rust writes.

- Net: writes + stamp live in separate transactions on separate connections → an interrupt introduces write/stamp desync → the observed `UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.address, pools.chain`.

### 3. The approaches (name + evaluate)

Evaluate; pick one as THE approach (with rationale); the others documented as considered-and-rejected.

**A. Move the whole update loop (chunk loop + RPC + writes + stamp) into Rust.** A Rust function (e.g. `run_pool_update(database_path, chain_id, exchange_specs, to_block, chunk_size, rpc_endpoint, ...) -> UpdateReport`) owns the whole run: chunk management, RPC event fetching, pool upserts, liquidity updates, stamp, single-transaction-per-chunk commit/rollback. The PyO3 seam is one call to start the run; Python boots the process + reports progress.

  - Sub-questions to resolve in the write-up:
    - **RPC layer in Rust:** the project's ADRs/AGENTS.md state RPC interaction is on the migration path (currently web3.py in Python). Does this epic do the RPC port as part of the chunk loop move (required — the chunk function needs to fetch its own events), OR does it call into an existing/partial Rust RPC crate? Inventory `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/` (referenced in AGENTS.md) for what's already there. If the RPC crate is real, use it; if not, this epic ports the minimum RPC needed (eth_getLogs, eth_blockNumber) into Rust as part of the work.

Decompose the chosen approach into implementation tasks to file as children of this epic. Each task ~1 commit with clear gates. For approach A, likely shape (refine in the write-up; the RPC sub-question drives the exact split):

1. **Rust RPC layer** (if not already present): eth_getLogs + eth_blockNumber + eth_getBlock in the `degenbot-rpc` crate (or wherever the project's RPC primitives live). If already present, this task is "verify + wire up."

## Architectural direction — this isn't a choice, it's AGENTS.md

**`AGENTS.md` §Architectural Vision** states the long-term goal explicitly: a set of first-class standalone Rust crates forming a complete, functional MEV bot — no Python required — where "that core must eventually own **everything** a functional MEV bot needs: pool/token state, swap math, event decoding, solvers, the pump loop, swap encoding, *and* the infrastructure currently still Python-only — **the database (persistence, not just ORM calls), RPC interaction, pub-sub, price oracles, the DB-aware pool and lending-market updaters**, simulation, and transaction submission. - **Atomicity invariant:** at chunk commit, EITHER (a) every pool row from `PoolCreated` events in the chunk + every liquidity update from `Mint`/`Burn` events in the chunk + the `last_update_block = working_end_block` stamp are ALL durably persisted (single transaction commit), OR (b) NONE of them are (single transaction rollback). No intermediate state is observable — including across an interrupt or crash.
- **Restart invariant:** `last_update_block` is a strict upper bound on the block range whose pool + liquidity data is durably committed. Restarting from `last_update_block + 1` re-processes only work that was NOT committed — never re-applies committed work.
- **No-duplicate-writer invariant:** at most one connection holds a write transaction on the DB during a chunk. (The current code violates this with multiple short-lived `DegenbotDb` connections + a SQLAlchemy session all writing concurrently.)

Reference the exact lines on `main` (git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py) where the invariant was held by construction: the shared `session` threaded through every updater, the ORM-dirty `exchange.last_update_block` stamp, the single `session.commit()` at chunk end.

### 2. The current regression (cite the code)

Document precisely how the invariant is broken in the current tree:
- `db_upsert_v3_pools` (and v2/v4) → own connection via `open_for_writes`; `upsert_v3_pools` (`rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs`) does per-row autocommit `execute()` with NO `transaction()` wrapper — pool rows durable mid-chunk, separate connection from the stamp.
- `db_apply_v3_liquidity_updates` / `db_apply_v4_liquidity_updates` — confirm the same pattern (separate connection; own writes). Read `rust/crates/degenbot-python/src/db/*.rs` for these seams.
- `db_set_exchange_last_update_block` — separate connection again.
- The SQLAlchemy `session.commit()` only commits SQLAlchemy-owned state, not the Rust writes.
- The per-call FFI + per-call connection pattern is both a bottleneck AND the source of the desync: each `db_*` call opens a fresh `DegenbotDb` connection, does its writes, and is gone — no connection/transaction spans the chunk.
- Net: writes + stamp live in separate transactions on separate connections → an interrupt introduces write/stamp desync → the observed `UNIQUE constraint failed: pools.address, pools.chain`.
- Frame this as a half-finished migration: the DB writes were moved to Rust core (good, per AGENTS.md), but the chunk-loop orchestration + RPC fetching + transaction ownership stayed in Python (the violation — that orchestration is standalone-usable logic stranded on the Python side, exactly what AGENTS.md's standalone-Rust-core constraint forbids).

### 3. THE approach (A) + the rejected alternatives (for the record)

**Approach A — Move the whole update loop (chunk loop + RPC + writes + stamp) into Rust.** AGENTS.md-mandated direction. A Rust function (e.g. `run_pool_update(database_path, chain_id, exchange_specs, to_block, chunk_size, rpc_endpoint, ...) -> UpdateReport`) owns the whole run: chunk management, RPC event fetching, pool upserts, liquidity updates, stamp, single-transaction-per-chunk commit/rollback. The PyO3 seam is ONE call to start the run; Python boots the process + reports progress. ADR-005 three-layer placement:
- **Rust core** (`degenbot-db` + `degenbot-rpc` + a new `pool-updater` module or crate): owns the chunk loop, the RPC fetches, the single connection + transaction, the writes, the stamp, the commit/rollback. Zero `pyo3` (enforced by `just check-no-pyo3-in-cores`).
- **PyO3 wrapper** (`degenbot-python/src/pool/`): `#[pyfunction] run_pool_update(...)` + a progress-callback type. Thin.
- **Python companion** (`cli/pool.py`): boot config → build exchange specs → call `run_pool_update` → report progress via the callback. No SQLAlchemy session, no per-call `db_*` dispatch, no tqdm on per-event Python iteration (tqdm ticks on callback).

  Sub-questions to resolve in the write-up:
    - **RPC layer in Rust:** AGENTS.md names "RPC interaction" as on the migration path AND lists `degenbot-rpc` among the core crates. **Inventory `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/`** to decide whether the RPC primitives the chunk loop needs (eth_getLogs, eth_blockNumber, eth_getBlock) already exist or must be ported as part of this epic. If `degenbot-rpc` is real, use it; if it's a stub, porting the minimum RPC the loop needs is IN SCOPE for this epic (per the standalone-Rust-core constraint — the loop can't strand its RPC fetches in Python web3.py).
    - **Progress reporting:** the current loop uses tqdm progress bars in Python. The Rust run must surface progress back (blocks processed, current chunk, pools added) — via a callback `#[pyfunction]` (called from Rust under the GIL) or a channel the Python side drains. Don't lose the UX; just move the loop.
    - **Exchange specs:** how are the per-chain exchange configs (factory addresses, event hashes, fee denominators, kind discriminators) passed to Rust? Currently `POOL_UPDATER[chain_id, exchange.name]` dispatches in Python. Preferred: Rust reads the exchanges table itself (the DB is the source of truth — AGENTS.md "Rust owns the state"), with a typed `ExchangeSpec` built at startup. Pass through FFI only what isn't in the DB (e.g. event-hash constants, though those could move to `degenbot-abi` / `degenbot-decoders`).
    - **Interrupt handling:** an interrupt (Ctrl-C / SIGINT) during the Rust run must abort cleanly, rolling back the current chunk's transaction. The `py.detach` GIL-release means Python-side KeyboardInterrupt won't pre-empt mid-chunk easily — the Rust run must poll for a cancel signal between chunks (or at chunk boundaries), honoring the interrupt between chunks while keeping each chunk atomic. State the contract precisely: "SIGINT between chunks: honored immediately. SIGINT mid-chunk: the current chunk completes (or its rollback runs) before the run returns."
    - **GIL discipline** (per `rust/AGENTS.md`): the chunk's RPC fetches + DB writes run GIL-released (`py.detach`); only the progress callback re-acquires the GIL. Long RPC polls must NOT hold the GIL.

**Approach B — Thread a single `DegenbotDb` connection through the existing `db_*` seams (don't rewrite the loop).** REJECTED: leaves the chunk-loop orchestration + RPC fetches in Python, which (a) is the bottleneck the orchestrator flagged, (b) strands standalone-usable logic on the Python side, violating AGENTS.md's standalone-Rust-core constraint, and (c) keeps Python as a co-implementation rather than a driver shell. Document for the record.

**Approach C — `INSERT OR IGNORE` / `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on pool inserts, without fixing the transaction structure.** REJECTED: papers over the duplicate-pool-insert symptom but leaves the write/stamp desync + double-applied liquidity (`apply_*_liquidity_updates` is stateful, not idempotent). Violates the atomicity invariant rather than restoring it. Document for the record.

**Approach D — Keep the loop in Python, wrap the chunk in one DB-level `BEGIN`..`COMMIT`.** REJECTED: leaks transaction handles across the FFI boundary (fragile rollback, murky cancel semantics), and still strands the loop logic on the Python side. Document for the record.

### 4. The implementation task decomposition

Decompose approach A into implementation tasks to file as children of this epic. Each task ~1 commit with clear gates. Likely shape (refine in the write-up; the §3 RPC-inventory sub-question drives the exact split):

1. **Rust RPC layer** (inventory `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/` first): eth_getLogs + eth_blockNumber + eth_getBlock, as a proper core crate (zero pyo3). If already present, this task becomes "wire up + extend to the chunk loop's needs." If absent, port the minimum RPC the loop needs (gated on the §3 inventory result).
2. **Exchange spec + event-config types in Rust**: the typed exchange configs (factory, event_hash, fee_denominator, kind) the chunk loop dispatches on. Rust reads the exchanges table itself where possible (DB is source of truth); constants like event hashes move to `degenbot-abi` / `degenbot-decoders`.
3. **`run_pool_update` Rust core function**: the chunk loop — progress-report root, chunk range computation, RPC event fetching (via #1), single-connection-per-chunk + single-transaction + pool upserts + liquidity updates + stamp + commit/rollback. Reuses the existing `upsert_v*_pools` / `apply_*_liquidity_updates` / `set_exchange_last_update_block` core logic but bound to the chunk's own connection.
4. **PyO3 seam + progress callback**: `run_pool_update(database_path, ..., progress_callback) -> UpdateReport`. GIL released across the run; progress reported via a `#[pyfunction]` callback (blocks processed, current chunk, pools added).
5. **Python CLI refactor**: `pool_update` becomes boot + hand-off (read config, build/omit exchange specs, call `run_pool_update`, report progress). Drop the SQLAlchemy session + the per-call `db_*` dispatch + the per-event Python tqdm iteration. tqdm stays but ticks on the callback.
6. **Regression test (contract artifact)**: reproduce the bug — chunk loop interrupts mid-chunk → assert the chunk is fully rolled back → restart re-processes cleanly with no `UNIQUE constraint` failure. This is the contract for the invariant.
7. **No-duplicate-writer test**: the chunk function holds a write transaction; a concurrent `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes` during the chunk blocks/refuses rather than producing concurrent writers.

File these as children of the epic with dependencies sequenced (1+2 before 3; 3 before 4; 4 before 5; 5 before 6+7). The orchestrator will create them from the write-up.

## Deliverable

A markdown file at `docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md` capturing:
- The invariant (§1).
- The current regression (§2, with code citations), framed as a half-finished migration that stranded the chunk-loop + RPC orchestration on the Python side.
- THE approach (A) + the rejected alternatives (§3), anchored in AGENTS.md's Architectural Vision language verbatim.
- The RPC-layer decision (port vs reuse existing `degenbot-rpc`) + the exact inventory of what Rust needs to fetch events.
- The implementation task decomposition (§4) — concrete enough that the orchestrator can file the tasks directly from it.

Commit it as `docs(migration): define pool-updater chunk atomicity invariant + fix approach`. Reference epic `2SFL6I`. Reference `main`'s chunk loop as the contract source of truth. Reference AGENTS.md §Architectural Vision.

## Constraints

- **Read `main` first** (`git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py`) — that's the contract. The current tree is the regression; `main` is the reference.
- **Inventory `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/`** (and any RPC primitives) — this decides whether the RPC layer needs porting as part of this epic or can be reused. The §3 RPC sub-question gates the §4 task split.
- Read the current Rust seams (`rust/crates/degenbot-python/src/db/*.rs`) + core (`rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs`, `connection.rs`) to cite the exact breakage points.
- Read `AGENTS.md` §Architectural Vision (the long-term goal + the standalone-Rust-core constraint + the explicit "database (persistence), RPC interaction, ... DB-aware pool ... updater" migration-path list) — ground the decision in this language. Also ADR-005 + ADR-003 (Bot as state owner) + the migration guide (`docs/migration-guides/three-layer-transition.md`) for the triage rubric.
- No code changes in this task — the write-up is the deliverable. The implementation tasks (filed separately after this lands) do the code.

## Report-back (to orchestrator t-6ff7 via link_send triggerTurn:true)

1. Commit hash of the write-up.
2. Confirmation approach A is the chosen direction (one-paragraph rationale anchored in AGENTS.md).
3. The RPC-layer decision (port eth_getLogs/etc into Rust as part of this epic, or reuse an existing `degenbot-rpc` crate — with the inventory result that drove it).
4. The list of implementation tasks you decomposed (titles + one-line summaries + dependencies) — so the orchestrator can file them as epic children directly.
5. Any sub-question from §3 you couldn't resolve + why.

## Result

Committed `35624d6f` — `docs(database): pool-updater chunk atomicity invariant + fix`. Markdown lint passes.

### Chosen approach
**A — move the whole update loop into Rust.** Anchored in AGENTS.md §Architectural Vision: "the database (persistence), RPC interaction, ... the DB-aware pool ... updater" are all explicitly on the migration path; the standalone-Rust-core constraint forbids stranding the loop logic on the Python side. Python becomes a driver shell (boot + progress), not a co-implementation.

### RPC-layer decision
**REUSE `degenbot-rpc` — no port in scope.** Inventory confirmed (cross-checked by orchestrator): `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/` is a mature core crate with `AlloyProvider::new(rpc_url, max_retries)`, `get_block_number()`, `get_block(n)`, `get_logs(&LogFilter)`, and `fetch_logs_chunked(...)` (built-in big-range pagination + concurrency, on alloy 2.0 with transport-throttle). The only genuinely new Rust surface is a pure-Rust decode leaf (`alloy::Log` → `PoolCreated`-row input / `LiquidityUpdateEvent`) belonging in `degenbot-decoders` (decode-only, no state, no FFI).

### Implementation task decomposition (filed separately by orchestrator as children of `2SFL6I`)
1. Wire `degenbot-rpc` into the chunk loop's RPC needs + the decode leaf (no port). ← depends on nothing
2. `ExchangeSpec` + event-config types in Rust (Rust reads the `exchanges` table). ← depends on 1
3. `run_pool_update` Rust core fn: chunk loop, single conn + `transaction()` per chunk, cancel-poll at chunk boundaries. ← depends on 1+2
4. PyO3 seam + `ProgressCallback`. ← depends on 3
5. Python CLI refactor: `pool_update` = boot + hand-off. ← depends on 4
6. Regression test: chunk interrupt → full rollback → restart clean (the contract). ← depends on 5
7. No-duplicate-writer test. ← depends on 3

### Notable nuance (for Task 3)
`degenbot-rpc` is async (alloy/tokio); `degenbot-db` is sync (rusqlite). `run_pool_update` must bridge these (likely a tokio runtime inside the chunk fn, or `block_on` per RPC fetch into the sync write path). Orchestrator will flag this in the Task 3 brief.

## References
- docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md (the write-up)
- AGENTS.md §Architectural Vision; ADR-005; rust/AGENTS.md (GIL discipline)
- git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py (the contract source of truth)

data.body:
## Goal

The first Rust surface for the Rust-owned chunk updater (epic `2SFL6I`). No RPC porting — `degenbot-rpc` already has everything (`AlloyProvider`, `get_logs`, `fetch_logs_chunked`, `get_block_number`, `get_block`). This task wires it into the shape the chunk loop will consume + adds the ONE genuinely new Rust surface: a pure-Rust decode leaf from `alloy::Log` → the existing `V3PoolRowInput`/`V4PoolRowInput`/`LiquidityUpdateEvent` types.

## Read first
- `docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md` §3.2 (the RPC-layer decision) + §4 Task 1.
- `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/src/provider.rs` — `AlloyProvider::new(rpc_url, max_retries)`, `get_block_number`, `get_block`, `get_logs(&LogFilter)`, `fetch_logs_chunked(from, to, addresses, topics)`. Note: this crate is ASYNC (alloy/tokio).
- `rust/crates/degenbot-rpc/src/subscription.rs` — `pump_logs` (for the pubsub shape, in case useful as a reference).
- The existing row-input types: `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs` (`V2PoolRowInput`, `V3PoolRowInput`, `V4PoolRowInput`) + `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/liquidity_updater.rs` (`LiquidityUpdateEvent`).
- The Python event-hash + topic constants the decode leaf must reproduce: `src/degenbot/cli/pool_updater_configs.py` (the `event_hash` per exchange family) + `src/degenbot/abis/` (the V2/V3/V4 PoolCreated / Mint / Burn ABI signatures).

## Deliverable

1. **A decode leaf in `degenbot-decoders`** (or wherever V2/V3/V4 event decode lives — check `rust/crates/degenbot-decoders/src/`):
   - `decode_pool_created_event(log: &alloy::Log, family: PoolFamily) -> DecodedPoolCreated` — extracts `(token0, token1, fee, tick_spacing?, pool_address)` from the log topics+data per the family's `PoolCreated` signature. Returns a type that can be mapped to `V2PoolRowInput`/`V3PoolRowInput`/`V4PoolRowInput` by the chunk fn (Task 3).
   - `decode_liquidity_event(log: &alloy::Log) -> LiquidityUpdateEvent` (Mint/Burn; maps to the existing `LiquidityUpdateEvent` in `liquidity_updater.rs`).
   - Event-topic-hash constants for V2/V3/V4 PoolCreated / Mint / Burn (move from Python's `pool_updater_configs.py` into Rust constants — these are protocol-level, belong in core).
   - Pure functions. No state. No FFI. No `pyo3` (enforced by `just check-no-pyo3-in-cores`).

2. **A small "RPC fetcher" thin wrapper** (in `degenbot-rpc` or a new `pool-updater` core module — your call, justify it) that exposes the chunk loop's exact needs as a typed async API:
   - `fetch_pool_created_logs(provider, from_block, to_block, factory_address, family) -> Vec<DecodedPoolCreated>`
   - `fetch_liquidity_logs(provider, from_block, to_block, pool_addresses?) -> Vec<LiquidityUpdateEvent>`
   - These wrap `AlloyProvider::fetch_logs_chunked` + the decode leaf. The chunk fn (Task 3) will call them.

## Validation gates
- `cargo test -p degenbot-decoders` green (new decode-leaf unit tests: feed a known `alloy::Log` from a real `PoolCreated`/`Mint`/`Burn` event → assert the decoded fields match).
- `cargo test -p degenbot-rpc` green (existing tests unaffected; new fetcher wrapper has a round-trip test if feasible without a live node, else a decode-only test).
- `cargo clippy -p degenbot-decoders -p degenbot-rpc -- -D warnings` clean.
- `just check-no-pyo3-in-cores` green.

## Commit
`feat(rust): wire degenbot-rpc into chunk-loop shape + alloy::Log decode leaf` (scope `rust`). Reference epic `2SFL6I` + the migration guide + task 1. No `.ergo/` files. Rust core only — no PyO3 wrapper, no Python.

## Report-back (to orchestrator via link_send triggerTurn:true)
1. Commit hash.
2. Gate pass/fail.
3. Where the decode leaf lives (crate + module path) + where the fetcher wrapper lives (and why there).
4. The exact event-topic-hash constants you moved + their source (which Python file).
5. Any deviation.

data.title: run_pool_update Rust core fn — chunk loop, single conn + transaction per chunk, cancel-poll
data.body:
## Goal

The heart of the epic: the Rust core function that owns the whole chunk loop under ONE connection + ONE transaction per chunk. This is what restores the §1 atomicity/restart/no-duplicate-writer invariants structurally. Zero `pyo3`.

## Read first
- `docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md` §1 (the invariant — THE contract), §3.1 (approach A), §3.3 (sub-questions: progress, interrupt, GIL), §4 Task 3.
- `git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py` — `main`'s chunk loop is the contract source of truth (the chunk-range computation, the `exchanges_to_update` set, the end-of-chunk stamp+commit). Lines ~1687-1830.
- `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/discovery.rs` — `upsert_v2_pools`/`upsert_v3_pools`/`upsert_v4_pools` (the writes to REUSE, bound to the chunk's conn).
- `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/liquidity_updater.rs` — `apply_v3_liquidity_updates`/`apply_v4_liquidity_updates` (the liquidity writes; note the per-pool idempotency marker `liquidity_update_block`/`liquidity_update_log_index`).
- `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/ops.rs` — `set_exchange_last_update_block` (the stamp).
- `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/connection.rs` — `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes`, `lock()` (the `Mutex<Connection>`), the busy_timeout pragma.

## Deliverable

`pub fn run_pool_update(database_path, chain_id, to_block, chunk_size, rpc_url, cancel: Arc<AtomicBool>, progress: Arc<dyn ProgressSink>) -> Result<UpdateReport, DbError>` (refine the signature; `ProgressSink` is a Rust trait the PyO3 seam (Task 4) will bridge to a Python callback).

### The chunk loop (mirror `main`'s shape, but in Rust, under one conn + one tx per chunk)
1. Open ONE `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes(database_path)` — held for the WHOLE run (not per-call). This is the structural fix: one writer, no desync.
2. `load_active_exchange_specs(db, chain_id)` (Task 2, `SHFIGX`).
3. `initial_start_block = min(exchange.last_update_block + 1 for active exchanges)` (read fresh from the DB, NOT a stale ORM attribute — `main`'s `fresh_last_update_block` re-read pattern).
4. Resolve `last_block` from `to_block` via `AlloyProvider::get_block_number`/`get_block` (Task 1, `SBICJJ`).
5. **Chunk loop** (`while working_start_block <= last_block`):
   a. `working_end_block = min(last_block, working_start_block + chunk_size - 1, …per-exchange last_update_block caps)`.
   b. `exchanges_to_update = { spec for spec if last_update_block is None or == working_start_block - 1 }`.
   c. **`let tx = conn.transaction()?;`** — ONE transaction wrapping EVERYTHING below.
   d. For each exchange in `exchanges_to_update`: `fetch_pool_created_logs(...)` → `upsert_v*_pools(...)` bound to `tx` (NOT a fresh conn).
   e. V3 liquidity: `fetch_liquidity_logs(...)` → `apply_v3_liquidity_updates(...)` bound to `tx`.
   f. V4 liquidity: same, bound to `tx`.
   g. For each exchange in `exchanges_to_update`: `set_exchange_last_update_block(tx, exchange.id, working_end_block)`.
   h. **`tx.commit()?;`** — the single atomic commit. On ANY `?` error above, `tx` drops → rollback → chunk fully reverted → `last_update_block` unchanged → restart re-processes cleanly. This is THE invariant.
   i. `progress.report(...)` (chunk-complete callback — GIL-safe via the PyO3 bridge in Task 4; here just call the trait method).
   j. **Cancel-poll at chunk boundary**: `if cancel.load(Relaxed) { return Ok(partial_report); }` — honored BETWEEN chunks, never mid-chunk (a chunk once started completes atomically).
   k. `working_start_block = working_end_block + 1`.
6. Return `UpdateReport { blocks_processed, chunks_committed, pools_added, liquidity_updates_applied, … }`.

### Key invariants (assert in Task 6/7 tests; enforce here by construction)
- ONE `DegenbotDb` connection for the whole run.
- ONE `transaction()` per chunk wrapping ALL writes + the stamp.
- Cancel honored only at chunk boundaries.
- `last_update_block` advances iff the chunk's writes commit.

### Bridge note (resolve deliberately)
`degenbot-rpc` is async (alloy/tokio); `degenbot-db` is sync (rusqlite). `run_pool_update` must bridge: likely a `tokio::runtime::Runtime::new()` (or `Handle::current()` if the PyO3 seam provides a runtime) with `rt.block_on(fetch_logs(...))` between sync DB writes. **Decide the runtime strategy deliberately** (owned runtime inside the fn vs rely on a runtime the caller provides) + document it. Don't accidentally nest runtimes. This is the one genuinely subtle implementation question — flag it in your report-back if you need the orchestrator's call.

## Validation gates
- `cargo test -p <new-crate-or-module>` green: a test that runs `run_pool_update` against a mock RPC (or a recorded fixture of `alloy::Log`s) + a temp DB → asserts the chunk committed + `last_update_block` advanced + pools present.
- `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` clean.
- `just check-no-pyo3-in-cores` green.

## Depends on
Tasks `SBICJJ` (RPC fetcher + decode leaf) + `SHFIGX` (ExchangeSpec).

## Commit

data.title: Python CLI refactor — pool_update becomes boot + hand-off
data.body:
## Goal

Refactor `src/degenbot/cli/pool.py::pool_update` so Python only boots the process + reports progress. Drop the SQLAlchemy session-for-writes, the per-call `db_*` dispatch, the `fresh_last_update_block` workaround, the per-event Python tqdm iteration, and the stale `session.commit()`. The Rust `run_pool_update` (Task `QZHNZQ`) owns everything else.

## Read first
- `docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md` §3.1 (three-layer placement — Python companion's role) + §4 Task 5.
- `src/degenbot/cli/pool.py` — the current chunk loop (what to delete).
- `git show main:src/degenbot/cli/pool.py` — `main`'s tqdm UX (what to preserve, on the callback).

## Deliverable

`cli/pool.py::pool_update` becomes:
1. Read config (bot, chain_id, chunk_size, to_block, rpc_url from the config).
2. Install a SIGINT handler that sets the Rust cancel flag (exposed by Task `QZHNZQ`'s seam — likely a module-level `Arc<AtomicBool>` accessor or a `set_cancel()` pyfunction).
3. Build a `progress_callback` Python callable that ticks tqdm (the loop's progress bar updates on callback, not per-event Python iteration).
4. Call `degenbot_rs.run_pool_update(database_path, chain_id, to_block, chunk_size, rpc_url, progress_callback)`.
5. Report the `UpdateReport` summary at the end.

**Delete from `cli/pool.py`:** the `while True` chunk loop, the `working_start_block`/`working_end_block` computation, the `exchanges_to_update` set, the per-exchange `pool_updater(...)` dispatch, the `get_v3_liquidity_events`/`get_v4_liquidity_events` calls, the `apply_v*_liquidity_updates` calls, the `db_set_exchange_last_update_block` loop, the `session.commit()`, the SQLAlchemy session-for-writes, the `fresh_last_update_block` re-read workaround. All of this now lives in the Rust core.

**Keep in `cli/pool.py`:** the Click command surface (`@cli.command("update")`, `--chunk-size`, `--to-block` options), the config bootstrap, the tqdm UX (re-wired to the callback), the user-facing echo.

## Validation gates
- `just test-python` green (existing pool-update CLI tests updated to the new hand-off shape — they should assert the hand-off call + the report, not the old per-chunk Python logic).
- `just test-rust-python` green (261 passed).

data.title: No-duplicate-writer test: chunk fn holds exclusive write tx
data.body:
## Goal

Asserts the §1 no-duplicate-writer invariant: while `run_pool_update` holds a chunk's write transaction, a concurrent `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes` blocks/refuses (SQLite `BUSY` → the existing `busy_timeout=5000` pragma retries with a timeout) rather than producing a second concurrent writer. Guards against the multi-writer race that caused the original regression.

## Read first
- `docs/migration-guides/pool-updater-chunk-atomicity.md` §1 (no-duplicate-writer invariant).
- `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/connection.rs` — `busy_timeout` pragma, the `Mutex<Connection>` (in-process) + SQLite's file-level lock (cross-process).
- The Task `CKXCOB` core fn.

## Deliverable

A test (in the Rust core crate's test module, since this is about the Rust connection model) `test_chunk_holds_exclusive_write_transaction`:
1. Start `run_pool_update` on a thread (with a mock RPC + a cancel flag that trips after the first chunk's transaction begins but before it commits — so the chunk's `tx` is held open).
2. On the main thread, attempt `DegenbotDb::open_for_writes(same_path)` + a write → assert it either blocks (then succeeds after the chunk commits/rolls back) or returns `SQLITE_BUSY` (after `busy_timeout`). The KEY assertion: it does NOT produce a second concurrent writer that interleaves writes with the chunk's transaction.
3. Confirm the in-process `Mutex<Connection>` is NOT the only guard (a second `DegenbotDb` instance is a separate Mutex) — the SQLite file-level `BUSY`/`busy_timeout` is what serializes them. Assert this.

## Validation gates
- `cargo test -p <core-crate>` green.
- `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` clean.

## Depends on
Task `CKXCOB` (the core fn — need its transaction held open mid-chunk).

data.title: DB performance improvements (schema + SQL)
data.body:
# DB performance improvements (schema + SQL)

## Origin
Post-rustqlite transition review of `rust/crates/degenbot-db` (schema in `src/schema_head.sql`; SQL in `src/{read,write,ops,discovery,snapshot,pathfinding,aave,liquidity_updater,heal,migrate}.rs`). The original schema was authored via SQLAlchemy ORM with `index=True` on FK columns and several ORM-default indexes that are likely non-optimal.

## Shape of the work
This epic starts as **research only**: one `spike:` task per review suggestion, each validating the hypothesis against the actual SQL/indexes/queries before any code or migration lands.

**Each research task carries an explicit instruction:** if the research *validates* the suggestion, append one or more implementation/primitive ergo tasks to THIS epic (children of this container), sized as single atomic changes (one Alembic migration, or one Rust PR), with acceptance criteria + validation gates. If validation *refutes* the suggestion, mark the spike `done` with a `result` explaining why — no implementation task appended.

## Gating constraints (must respect)
- **Schema is Alembic-owned through the 0.6.x series** (ADR-010/ADR-011). Index drops/adds require a **new Alembic migration** and a bumped `ALEMBIC_HEAD` in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema.rs` — allowed in 0.6.x. Structural table changes (`WITHOUT ROWID`, column type changes, dropping columns) are **gated to 0.7** (Rust-owned schema cutover); gate those implementation tasks behind `JFFQV2` (0.7 retirement).
- **`PRAGMA foreign_keys` is never set ON** in the open path (`connection.rs` sets only `WAL/busy_timeout/synchronous/query_only`). FK declarations are non-enforced → FK-column indexes matter only for query performance, never for referential integrity.
- Rust-only query changes (no migration) are actionable now regardless of the 0.6.x gating.

## Reference paths
- Schema DDL: `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema_head.sql`
- Schema constants: `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema.rs`
- Open PRAGMAs: `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/connection.rs` (`PRE_SCHEMA_PRAGMAS`)
- Hot path (liquidity updater): `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/liquidity_updater.rs`
- ADRs: `docs/adr/ADR-010-*.md`, `docs/adr/ADR-011-*.md`

data.title: spike: drop 9 redundant leftmost-prefix FK indexes
data.body:
# spike: drop 9 redundant leftmost-prefix FK indexes

## Goal
- Confirm that 9 single-column FK indexes are redundant (their lookup is served as the leftmost prefix of an existing UNIQUE composite index) and can be dropped, cutting write amplification + storage on the affected tables.

## Hypothesis (from the post-rustqlite review)
Each of these single-column indexes duplicates the leftmost column of an existing UNIQUE index, so SQLite's leftmost-prefix rule serves the same predicate from the composite. They are pure write-amplification (every INSERT/UPDATE writes two B-trees) with no query benefit.

| Drop | Already served by (leftmost prefix) |
|------|-------------------------------------|
| `ix_aave_v3_asset_configs_asset_id` | `ix_aave_asset_config_asset` UNIQUE(`asset_id`) |
| `ix_aave_v3_assets_underlying_asset_id` | `ix_aave_assets_underlying_asset_market` UNIQUE(`underlying_asset_id`, `market_id`) |
| `ix_aave_v3_collateral_positions_user_id` | `ix_aave_collateral_position_user_asset` UNIQUE(`user_id`, `asset_id`) |
| `ix_aave_v3_debt_positions_user_id` | `ix_aave_debt_position_user_asset` UNIQUE(`user_id`, `asset_id`) |
| `ix_aave_v3_emode_categories_market_id` | `ix_aave_emode_category_market_cat` UNIQUE(`market_id`, `category_id`) |
| `ix_aave_v3_user_collateral_configs_user_id` | `ix_aave_user_collateral_config_user_asset` UNIQUE(`user_id`, `asset_id`) |
| `ix_pools_token0_id` | `ix_liquidity_pools_token_ids` (`token0_id`, `token1_id`) |
| `ix_managed_pool_liquidity_positions_managed_pool_id` | `ix_managed_pool_liquidity_positions_pool_id_tick` UNIQUE(`managed_pool_id`, `tick`) |
| `ix_managed_pool_initialization_maps_managed_pool_id` | `ix_managed_pool_initialization_maps_pool_id_word` UNIQUE(`managed_pool_id`, `word`) |

## What to investigate
1. For each row above, confirm in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema_head.sql` that the serving UNIQUE index's leftmost column equals the dropped index's column.
2. Grep every SQL predicate in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/**/*.rs` that filters on the dropped column ALONE (e.g. `WHERE user_id = ?` without `asset_id`). If any such predicate exists and is not a prefix of the composite, that index is NOT redundant — keep it and note which one.
3. For each kept-UNIQUE serving index, confirm it is actually unique and not just a non-unique composite (leftmost-prefix is served by non-unique composites too, so uniqueness is not required — but confirm the serving index exists at all).
4. Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on a representative lookup against a fixture DB (e.g. `rust/crates/degenbot-db/tests/fixtures/*.db`) to confirm SQLite picks the composite index for `WHERE <col> = ?` after the drop.

## Validation
- For each of the 9: a one-line verdict REDUNDANT (drop) or KEEP (with the predicate that needs it).
- The grep results of every predicate touching each column.

## Gating constraint
Index drops require a new Alembic migration + `schema_head.sql` mirror + `ALEMBIC_HEAD` bump — allowed in 0.6.x. Implementation tasks NOT gated to 0.7.

## If validated → append implementation tasks
If research confirms the suggestion, append one or more implementation tasks to epic `F4N6DX` (DB performance improvements). Each appended task:
- is a single atomic change (one Alembic migration OR one Rust PR);
- includes concrete Acceptance Criteria + Validation Gates (exact `just`/`cargo`/`sql` commands);
- for schema/index changes: ships a new Alembic migration under `src/degenbot/migrations/versions/`, mirrors the DDL change in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema_head.sql`, and bumps `ALEMBIC_HEAD` in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema.rs`;
- is sequenced after this spike (`ergo sequence <THIS-SPIKE-ID> <IMPL-ID>`);
- respects the gating constraint noted below.

If research refutes the suggestion, mark THIS spike `done` with a `result` summarising why — do NOT append an implementation task.

# spike: drop low-selectivity boolean index ix_aave_user_collateral_config_enabled

## Goal
- Confirm `ix_aave_user_collateral_config_enabled` (an index on a BOOLEAN column of `aave_v3_user_collateral_configs`) is never used by the planner and can be dropped.

## Hypothesis
A boolean column has ~50% selectivity; the SQLite planner will always prefer a full table scan over such an index, so it is pure write-amplification with no read benefit.

## What to investigate
1. Confirm the index exists in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/schema_head.sql`.

4. Build a representative fixture DB (or reuse `tests/fixtures/aave_parity.db`) with a non-trivial row count and run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT ... WHERE enabled = 1` to confirm the planner does a full scan (not the index). Vary row count (100 / 1000 / 10000) — boolean selectivity can shift planner choice at small N.

## Validation

data.title: spike: add pools(chain, kind) index for chain-scoped reads
data.body:
# spike: add pools(chain, kind) index for chain-scoped reads

## Goal
- Determine whether a `pools(chain, kind)` (or `pools(chain)`) index materially speeds up the chain-scoped reads on `pools` that filter by `chain` (and sometimes `kind IN (...)`), and whether the planner will actually use it.

## Hypothesis
Several reads filter `WHERE chain = ?` on `pools` with no index whose leftmost column is `chain`:
- `fetch_pools_for_chain` (`read.rs`)
- `fetch_v3_pool_addresses` (`snapshot.rs`)
- V3 branch of `fetch_all_liquidity_maps` (`snapshot.rs`)
- V2/V3 branch of `fetch_path_graph_edges` + `fetch_tokens_with_min_degree` (`pathfinding.rs`)

`ix_liquidity_pool_address_chain` is UNIQUE(`address`, `chain`) — `chain` alone is NOT a leftmost prefix, so these are full table scans today. A `pools(chain, kind)` index lets the planner skip V2 rows for the V3-family `kind IN (...)` reads.

## What to investigate
1. Enumerate every `pools` predicate across `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/**/*.rs` + the Python `src/degenbot/**` that filters on `chain` and/or `kind`. Record the exact predicate shape for each.
2. Judge the result-set fraction: for the chain-scoped reads that return a LARGE fraction of a chain's pools (e.g. `fetch_pools_for_chain`, the pathfinding edges), a full scan may legitimately beat an index. For the `kind IN ('uniswap_v3', ...)` reads that skip V2 rows, an index is more likely to help. Separate the two cases.
3. Build a representative fixture DB (or synthesize one) with a realistic mix of V2 + V3 pools per chain and run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on each predicate under: (a) no new index, (b) `pools(chain)`, (c) `pools(chain, kind)`. Record which plan wins.
4. Decide between `pools(chain)` and `pools(chain, kind)` based on the observed plan + the query shapes (covering-index benefit for the `kind IN` reads).
5. Measure (rough is fine): does any read here appear in a hot path (per-tx / per-backrun) or only construction-time (startup)? Construction-time reads tolerate a full scan; do NOT add an index whose only benefit is a one-off startup read.

# spike: prepare_cached in liquidity-updater hot loop

## Goal
- Confirm that switching `conn.prepare(sql)` → `conn.prepare_cached(sql)` in the liquidity-updater hot path is correct (statements are re-entrant / not held across conflicting borrows) and reduces per-pool statement-compilation CPU.

## Hypothesis
`rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/liquidity_updater.rs` compiles a fresh prepared statement PER POOL inside one chunk `Transaction` in: `fetch_v3_liquidity_map_on_conn`, `fetch_v4_liquidity_map_on_conn`, the upsert chunk loops (`upsert_v3/v4_liquidity_positions_on_conn`, `upsert_v3/v4_initialization_maps_on_conn`), `delete_stale_*_on_conn`, and the `set_*_liquidity_update_marker_on_conn` UPDATEs. `prepare_cached` lets rusqlite's per-connection statement cache amortize compilation across the whole chunk.

## What to investigate
1. Enumerate every `conn.prepare(...)` site in `liquidity_updater.rs` (Rust). For each, record the SQL string + whether the prepared statement is held alive while another statement on the SAME connection runs (rusqlite forbids two concurrent immutable borrows of cached statements that alias the same connection — verify each call's borrow scope).
2. Check rusqlite's `prepare_cached` re-entrancy rules: a cached statement borrowed via `prepare_cached` must be dropped before another statement (cached or not) is stepped on the SAME connection, UNLESS using `unchecked` variants. Map each site to whether the current borrow structure already satisfies this (most do — they `query_map` to completion and drop before the next call).
3. For the dynamically-built upsert SQL (placeholders vary by chunk size), confirm `prepare_cached` keys on the exact SQL text — meaning chunking to bucket sizes would fragment the cache. Decide whether to (a) accept cache fragmentation, or (b) pad to fixed chunk sizes for cache hits. Recommend.
4. Decide whether to extend the change to the read fns in `read.rs` / `snapshot.rs` called in loops (lower priority; the updater is the hot path).

## Validation
- Per site: verdict SAFE-FOR-CACHED / NEEDS-RESHAPE (with the reason: e.g. concurrent borrow).
- A recommended scope (which sites to convert; whether to bucket chunk sizes).
- A rough estimate of compilations saved per chunk (number of pools × statements-per-pool).

# spike: tidy delete_stale_rows chunked placeholder rebuild

## Goal
- Confirm the chunked-path placeholder string-rebuild in `delete_stale_rows` (`liquidity_updater.rs`) is correct for non-divisible chunk counts and rewrite it to build the per-chunk SQL directly from `chunk.len()` instead of `str::replace`-ing the full-list template.

## Hypothesis
`delete_stale_rows` pre-builds the SQL with `sql_placeholders_for(live_keys.len())`, then PER CHUNK does `sql.replace(&sql_placeholders_for(live_keys.len()), &placeholders)` to swap in the chunk-sized placeholder list. data.body:
# spike: WITHOUT ROWID + drop vestigial id on tick/init-map tables (0.7-gated)

## Goal
- Validate that converting the four tick/init-map tables to `WITHOUT ROWID` with a composite `PRIMARY KEY (pool_id, tick|word)` (dropping the vestigial `id` rowid-alias column) is safe — meaning no query filters/joins on `id` — and worth it (halves write amplification on these, the largest tables).

## Hypothesis
Tables: `liquidity_positions`, `initialization_maps`, `managed_pool_liquidity_positions`, `managed_pool_initialization_maps`. Today each is a rowid table with `PRIMARY KEY (id)` (rowid alias) + a separate `UNIQUE(pool_id, tick|word)` index B-tree. The `id` column is vestigial — the read fns `SELECT id, …` but EVERY predicate is `pool_id`/`tick`/`word`. `WITHOUT ROWID` + composite PK merges the rowid table + the unique index into ONE B-tree ordered by `(pool_id, tick|word)`: halves INSERT/UPDATE B-tree writes; the `WHERE pool_id = ? ORDER BY tick` range scan becomes a single sequential read.

## What to investigate
1. Grep EVERY occurrence of the `id` column of these four tables across `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/**/*.rs` + `src/degenbot/**` + the parity tests. Confirm `id` is never used in a `WHERE`, `JOIN … ON`, `ORDER BY`, or returned to callers as a stable key. (The read fns SELECT it but presumably discard it — confirm the row structs expose it and whether anyone reads the field.)
2. Check the heal/dump-and-restore path (`heal.rs`) + `ops.rs::create_new_database`: a `WITHOUT ROWID` table has NO `sqlite_sequence` and no rowid — confirm the heal copy loop (`SELECT … FROM old → INSERT INTO new`) does not depend on a rowid or `sqlite_sequence` reset for these tables. (It resets `sqlite_sequence` per table — that step is a no-op for `WITHOUT ROWID` tables, which is fine, but confirm.)
3. Check whether any FK elsewhere references `liquidity_positions.id` etc. (None should — these are leaf tables; confirm via `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` on every other table.)
4. Confirm the composite UNIQUE indexes (`ix_liquidity_positions_pool_id_tick` etc.) become the `PRIMARY KEY` and the separate single-column `_managed_pool_id` indexes are the R1 redundancy-drop targets (do NOT bundle — R8 only validates the WITHOUT ROWID restructure; the index drop is R1's scope).
5. Estimate the storage + write-CPU win on a representative large DB (synthesize one or reuse a fixture seeded large): rowid table + unique index vs single WITHOUT ROWID table.

## Validation
- Verdict: `id` is provably vestigial (every reference enumerated + shown non-load-bearing) OR a real dependency exists (list it; the restructure is blocked).
- Heal-path compatibility: Y/N with the specific assertion.
- A before/after storage + write-CPU measurement on a large fixture.

## Gating constraint
**Structural table change — gated to 0.7** (Rust-owned schema cutover; ADR-010/ADR-011). Implementation tasks appended from this spike MUST be blocked behind `JFFQV2` (0.7 retirement) and ideally land as part of the Rust-owned head schema (not an Alembic migration — Alembic cannot express `WITHOUT ROWID` cleanly; this rides the dump-and-restore cutover).

data.body:
# spike: VARCHAR(78) → BLOB(32) for uint256 columns (0.7-gated)

## Goal
- Decide whether converting the `VARCHAR(78)` decimal-string uint256 columns to fixed 32-byte `BLOB` is worth it: ~1.5–2.4× smaller for the big tables, better cache density, but touches every encode/decode site + every parity fixture.

## Hypothesis
The uint256 columns (`liquidity_net`, `liquidity_gross`, `bitmap` on the tick/init-map tables; Aave `balance`, `liquidity_index`, `borrow_index`, `liquidity_rate`, `borrow_rate`, `debt_ceiling`, `isolation_mode_debt`, `stk_aave_balance`, `bitmap`) are stored as decimal strings (1–78 bytes, variable). A 32-byte `BLOB` is smaller and fixes width. Trade-off: decimal strings are human-inspectable and the comparison semantics are different (lexicographic-vs-numeric, though these columns are not used in range/order predicates today).

## What to investigate
1. Enumerate EVERY `VARCHAR(78)` column in `schema_head.sql` + its Python model (`src/degenbot/database/models/**`) — the `IntMappedToString` `TypeDecorator`. Categorize: actually-uint256 vs signed (`liquidity_net` is signed → I256 → must encode sign in 32 bytes or keep a separate sign).
2. Enumerate every encode/decode site in `rust/crates/degenbot-db/src/rows/decode.rs` + the liquidity_updater (`encode_u256`/`decode_u256`/`encode_i256`/`decode_i256`) + the Aave writer. Quantify the blast radius.
3. Check the parity fixtures (`tests/fixtures/*_expected.json`) — they assert VALUES not byte encoding (decimal-string vs BLOB would change the row bytes but the decoded value is identical). Confirm whether the parity harness reads the column via SQL or via the Rust decode (the latter is encoding-agnostic; the former would break).
4. Decide the signed-value encoding for I256 (`liquidity_net`): two's-complement 32-byte big-endian is the natural choice; confirm alloy `I256` round-trips through it.
5. Estimate storage + cache-density win on the largest tables (`liquidity_positions` / `managed_pool_liquidity_positions`) — net/gross are stored as VARCHAR; for typical 128-bit values the VARCHAR is ~39 bytes, vs 32 bytes BLOB; for small values (single-digit net) VARCHAR is ~2 bytes vs 32 bytes BLOB (BLOB is WORSE for small values). Decide whether the win is real for the actual value distributions (gross liquidity is typically large; net can be small).
6. Recommendation: BLOB for `bitmap` (always 32 bytes, big win — VARCHAR(78) for a full uint256 is 78 bytes) + `liquidity_gross` (large values); keep VARCHAR for `liquidity_net` if values skew small. OR skip entirely if the distributions make it a wash.

## Validation
- Per-column verdict: CONVERT / KEEP, with the value-distribution justification.
- The signed-encoding decision for I256 (if converting `liquidity_net`).
- A storage measurement on a representative large fixture for the convert-worthy columns.

## Gating constraint
**Column type change — gated to 0.7** (same reasoning as R8: rides the dump-and-restore cutover). Implementation tasks appended from this spike MUST be blocked behind `JFFQV2`.

This is a **decision-heavy** spike, not a slam-dunk. The explicit deliverable is the recommendation + per-column verdict, not code.

data.title: spike: reconcile empty-live_keys prune semantics in delete_stale_rows
data.body:
# spike: reconcile empty-live_keys prune semantics in delete_stale_rows

## Goal
- Resolve the comment/code mismatch in `delete_stale_rows` (`liquidity_updater.rs`): the comment says "delete ALL rows for this pool" but the code `return Ok(())` on `live_keys.is_empty()` deletes nothing. Decide whether this is a real bug or faithful parity-with-Python, and what the correct behaviour is.

## Hypothesis (correctness, surfaced during the perf review)
When an apply drives every tick's liquidity to zero, `tick_data` is empty → `live_ticks` empty → `persist_v3`/`persist_v4` calls `delete_stale_*_on_conn(conn, pool_id, &[])`. `delete_stale_rows` early-returns without deleting, so the now-zero positions linger as stale rows. The upsert path (`upsert_v3_liquidity_positions_on_conn`) ALSO early-returns on empty `tick_data`, so nothing corrects it. Net effect: a pool whose liquidity fully drains may retain ghost tick rows in the DB.

## What to investigate
1. Read `delete_stale_rows` + the comment + the two early returns (delete + upsert) in `liquidity_updater.rs`.
2. Find the PYTHON oracle this ports: `cli/pool.py::apply_v3/v4_liquidity_updates` — locate the `delete(...).where(pool_id==?, tick.in_(ticks_to_drop))` call. Determine what `ticks_to_drop` is when the live set is empty:
   - If `ticks_to_drop` is the COMPLEMENT of the live set (i.e. `existing_ticks - live_ticks`), an empty live set → `ticks_to_drop = all existing ticks` → the Python DELETES everything. The Rust early-return is then a BUG (parity violation).
   - If `ticks_to_drop` is derived such that empty-live is a no-op in Python too, the Rust is parity-faithful and only the COMMENT is wrong.
3. Walk `persist_v3`/`persist_v4`: `live_ticks = tick_data.keys().copied().collect()` (the LIVE set), passed as `live_keys` to `delete_stale_*` whose SQL is `DELETE ... WHERE pool_id = ?1 AND tick NOT IN (live_keys)`. With `live_keys` empty, `NOT IN ()` is vacuously TRUE → "delete all" is the SEMANTICALLY CORRECT behaviour; the early-return PREVENTS it. So the code is bugged and the comment is right.
4. Build a minimal repro: a fixture pool with some tick rows, apply events that zero out every tick, confirm the Rust leaves ghost rows while the intended semantic (and presumably Python) deletes them. If Python also leaves them, this is a deeper pre-existing bug to flag, not a Rust regression.
5. Decide the fix: remove the `live_keys.is_empty()` early return in `delete_stale_rows` and instead branch to `DELETE FROM {table} WHERE {id_col} = ?1` (no `NOT IN` clause) when empty, OR keep the early return + fix the comment if Python is also a no-op.
6. Note: this is NOT a perf issue — it's a correctness finding hit during the review. It is small and self-contained; if validated as a bug, the appended implementation task is a one-line-ish fix + a regression test.

## Validation
- The Python oracle's `ticks_to_drop` derivation + its behaviour on empty-live.
- A repro test (pass/fail) showing the Rust vs intended behaviour.
- Verdict: BUG (fix) or PARITY-FAITHFUL (fix comment only).

## Gating constraint
Rust-only fix, no migration — actionable now (0.6.x). Possibly a one-line fix + regression test once determined.

## If validated → append implementation tasks

# Drop 9 redundant leftmost-prefix FK indexes

## Goal
- Drop 9 single-column FK indexes that duplicate the leftmost column of an existing UNIQUE/composite index, cutting write amplification + storage on the affected tables (incl. the largest: `managed_pool_liquidity_positions`, `managed_pool_initialization_maps`).

## Origin

# Drop 10 redundant/dead-weight indexes (Alembic migration + mirror + model changes)

## Goal
Drop 10 single-column indexes that are either (a) redundant leftmost-prefix duplicates of an existing UNIQUE/composite index, or (b) dead-weight with zero read predicates. Cuts write amplification + storage on the affected tables (incl. the largest: `managed_pool_liquidity_positions`, `managed_pool_initialization_maps`).

## Origin
Validated by two completed spikes under this epic:
- `R3SR7L` → indexes #1–#9 (all redundant leftmost-prefix duplicates)
- `ULMN4U` → index #10 (dead-weight hand-declared index, zero read predicates)

## The 10 indexes

### Group A — redundant leftmost-prefix duplicates (origin: spike R3SR7L, ORM `index=True` cruft)
1. `ix_aave_v3_asset_configs_asset_id` — served by `ix_aave_asset_config_asset` UNIQUE(`asset_id`)
2. `ix_aave_v3_assets_underlying_asset_id` — served by `ix_aave_assets_underlying_asset_market` UNIQUE(`underlying_asset_id`, `market_id`)
3. `ix_aave_v3_collateral_positions_user_id` — served by `ix_aave_collateral_position_user_asset` UNIQUE(`user_id`, `asset_id`)
4. `ix_aave_v3_debt_positions_user_id` — served by `ix_aave_debt_position_user_asset` UNIQUE(`user_id`, `asset_id`)
5. `ix_aave_v3_emode_categories_market_id` — served by `ix_aave_emode_category_market_cat` UNIQUE(`market_id`, `category_id`)
6. `ix_aave_v3_user_collateral_configs_user_id` — served by `ix_aave_user_collateral_config_user_asset` UNIQUE(`user_id`, `asset_id`)
7. `ix_pools_token0_id` — served by `ix_liquidity_pools_token_ids` (`token0_id`, `token1_id`) [non-unique; leftmost-prefix works on non-unique]
8. `ix_managed_pool_liquidity_positions_managed_pool_id` — served by UNIQUE(`managed_pool_id`, `tick`)
9. `ix_managed_pool_initialization_maps_managed_pool_id` — served by UNIQUE(`managed_pool_id`, `word`)

### Group B — dead-weight hand-declared index (origin: spike ULMN4U)
10. `ix_aave_user_collateral_config_enabled` — boolean-column index, **zero read predicates filter on `enabled`** anywhere in the codebase (Rust or Python). Dead weight in practice.

## Rationale corrections from the research (preserve in implementation notes)
- **Leftmost-prefix rule (Group A):** the original "lone-column predicate → KEEP" framing was theoretically WRONG. SQLite serves `WHERE A=?` from a composite on `(A,B)` just as well as a single-col on `A`. EXPLAIN confirmed no planner regression for #3/#4/#6 (the lone `user_id` predicates at aave.rs:178/243/289) after dropping — the planner picks the serving composite. Drop all 9.
- **Selectivity heuristic (Group B):** the original hypothesis ("planner prefers full scan over a 50%-selectivity boolean index") is FALSE for SQLite — SQLite picks the index regardless of selectivity at every N tested (100/1000/10000, incl. after ANALYZE and 90/10 skew). The deciding evidence for #10 is NOT selectivity but the total absence of any `WHERE enabled` predicate. Rationale in the migration comment must cite "no read predicate uses this index," NOT "low selectivity."

## CRITICAL model-side change has TWO distinct mechanics (the trap)

The implementation has TWO different model-side fixes depending on the index origin:

### Group A (#1–#9): column-level `index=False` override — NOT alias-level
These 9 come from SQLAlchemy `index=True` on SHARED FK-column aliases (`ForeignKeyAaveAssetId`, `ForeignKeyTokenId`, `ForeignKeyAaveUserId`, `ForeignKeyAaveMarketId`, `ForeignKeyManagedPoolId`) reused across MULTIPLE tables. Naively stripping `index=True` from the alias would OVER-DROP the single-col index on sibling tables where that column is the **2nd** composite column (NOT a leftmost prefix) and is therefore genuinely needed (e.g. `ix_aave_v3_collateral_positions_asset_id`, `ix_pools_token1_id`, `ix_aave_v3_contracts_market_id`).

**Do NOT** strip `index=True` at the alias / shared-type level. Apply a column-level `index=False` override on each of the 9 specific columns in their model classes (`src/degenbot/database/models/aave.py` + `pools.py`). This neutralises the alias's `index=True` for that one column only.

### Group B (#10): delete the standalone `Index(...)` block — NOT a column override
This index is a deliberate hand-declared `Index("ix_aave_user_collateral_config_enabled", AaveV3UserCollateralConfig.enabled)` block in `src/degenbot/database/models/aave.py:558-561`. The column itself (`enabled: Mapped[bool]` at aave.py:523) has NO `index=True` to flip. Just delete the `Index(...)` declaration block. (Original creation already in `migrations/versions/9c411aeeb15e_aave_v3_extend_schema.py:101`.)

Sibling indexes NOT in either list above are correctly EXCLUDED — verify none regress (2nd-column / no-composite cases).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] New Alembic migration under `src/degenbot/migrations/versions/<new_rev>.py` whose `upgrade()` is 10× `op.drop_index(...)` and whose `downgrade()` is 10× `op.create_index(...)` mirroring the original definitions in `schema_head.sql`. ## Sequencing + Bundling decision
Bundled ULMN4U into this single migration (one `ALEMBIC_HEAD` bump carrying all 10 drops) rather than shipping two revisions. Sequenced after both spikes (`R3SR7L`, `ULMN4U`), both now done.

## Gating
